paper.title: Gender gaps in the effects of childhood family environment: Do they persist into adulthood?
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference is given. …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish administrative data covering the entire population born in Denmark between 1966 and 1995 (data from 1980 to 2015)
registers.role: sample frame, treatment (parental education and family structure), outcomes (education, employment, earnings), controls, linkage to parents and siblings
treatment (parental marital status at birth); prenatal inputs and birth outcomes in Appendix Table A.3
outcomes (behavioral and emotional disorder diagnoses; pregnancy complications)
variables_mentioned: ICD-10 codes F90-98 (behavioral and emotional disorder)
preeclampsia, gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes mellitus

registers.name_in_paper: administrative data on grade 9 GPA (begins in 2002) and on special education (observed for 2007-2011)
variables_mentioned: grade 9 GPA (teacher assessment and final exams)

linkages: each child is linked to his or her biological parents (both mother and father) and to siblings
full siblings are defined as children with the same mother and the same father
individuals are tracked over time with whom they live, giving family structure at age 12 (measured on January 1st of the year the child turns 13)
marital status at birth comes from the medical birth registry, which begins in 1973

sample.universe: The entire population born in Denmark between 1966 and 1995
sample.unit_of_observation: individual (child), observed at a given age; the sibling sample compares brothers and sisters within the same family
selection_rules: individuals born in Denmark between 1966 and 1995 (1973-1995 for the main analysis)

restrict to those for whom all parental variables are observed (mother's education missing for 1.28 percent, father's education for 2.96 percent of children who would otherwise be in the total population sample)
include only families without adopted children
require an observation on grade 9 completion on time (for the samples in Table 1)
sibling sample: additionally require at least one biological full sibling in the sample

cohorts differ by outcome: 1986-1995 for grade 9 outcomes, 1991-1995 for special education, 1973-1984 for outcomes at age 31, 1966-1984 for educational attainment across cohorts, 1966-1971 for labor market outcomes at ages 26/31/36/41
sample.n_observations: 1,472,204 entire population; 1,289,542 total population sample; 888,635 sibling sample (individuals born 1973-1995 with an observation on grade 9 completion on time)

construction_notes: parental education grouped into three categories: less than 12 years (< HS), high school graduate (HS, may include some vocational training or two year college), and bachelor's degree or more (BA, including professional bachelor degrees)
for the sibling sample, parents' marital status is measured at the birth of the youngest of their joint children; only married vs non-married is distinguished
family structure at age 12 is measured on January 1st of the year the child turns 13, distinguishing traditional (both biological parents), step-parent and single-parent families
grade 9 GPA is an average of all grades from teacher assessment and final exams, standardized to mean zero and standard deviation one by year of grade 9 completion for the entire population
behavioral and emotional disorder requires at least one hospital diagnosis (ICD-10 F90-98) by age 21; 92 percent of those with a diagnosis by age 21 received it by age 16
highest completed education is measured in months
earnings are expressed as the annual labor earnings percentile by year of birth and gender, following Chetty et al. (2014), so that individuals with zero earnings are included
employment is defined as having any positive labor earnings or employment as the main source of income, including self-employment
maternal age at birth enters linear, squared and cubed; standard errors are clustered at the family level
estimates in all tables except highest completed education (months) are multiplied by 100

claims.statement: In a balance regression of an indicator for the child being male on observed family characteristics, # of children in family is associated with a 0.25 percentage points difference in the probability that the child is male (the total population sample, cohorts 1973–1995).

definition.value: Number of children in the family, entered as a regressor in a balance regression whose dependent variable is an indicator for the child being male.

timing.value: measured in the family of origin

definition.value: An indicator for the child being male, used as the dependent variable in a balance regression of child gender on observed family characteristics.

timing.value: at birth

units.value: percentage points of the probability that the child is male (the table note states that all estimates are multiplied by 100)

estimand.target_population: The association between observed family characteristics and the probability that a child is male, in the total population sample (birth cohorts 1973–1995).

population.description: Individuals born in Denmark in the total population sample (not twins, not adopted, singleton births, all parental variables observed), birth cohorts 1973–1995.
population.period: Danish administrative data on the entire population of Denmark from 1980 to 2015
subgroups_defined: parents married / not married at birth
traditional / step-parent / single-parent family at age 12
population.selection: Individuals born in Denmark who are not twins and not adopted, are singleton births, and for whom all parental variables (including both parents' education) are observed.

identification.source_of_variation: None: the regression describes whether observed family characteristics differ for boys and girls (a balance check on the randomness of child gender).

key_assumptions.assumption: No identifying assumption is invoked: Table 2 is a balance test that regresses an indicator for the child being male on observed family characteristics to check whether boys and girls are selected into different family types.
key_assumptions.supported_by: joint F-tests reported in the table (Prob > F1 and Prob > F2)

claims.statement: Boys differ from girls in Grade 9 On Time by -9.3 percentage points, conditional on the model's controls and fixed effects (the total population sample, cohorts 1986–1995).

definition.value: Indicator for the child being male; the omitted category is female. In the regressions reported here it is the base male-female gap for children in the omitted family-environment categories (less than HS educated parents, non-married parents, single-parent family at age 12).

timing.value: at birth

definition.value: Indicator for whether the person completed grade 9 by age 16. The first nine years of schooling in Denmark are mandatory primary school; children are required to start first grade the year they turn 7. The paper describes it as "a marker of academic achievement that reflects a combination of early school readiness and success in school progression".

timing.value: measured at age 16; grade 9 outcomes are measured at age 15 for about half of the sample, since the school year ends in June

units.value: percentage points (the table note states that all estimates are multiplied by 100)

magnitude.interpretation: boys are 9.3 percentage points less likely to complete grade 9 on time than girls

estimand.target_population: The conditional male-female gap in Grade 9 On Time in the total population sample (birth cohorts 1986–1995).

population.description: Individuals born in Denmark in the total population sample (not twins, not adopted, singleton births, all parental variables observed), birth cohorts 1986–1995.
population.ages: measured at age 16; grade 9 outcomes are measured at age 15 for about half of the sample, since the school year ends in June

population.selection: Individuals born in Denmark who are not twins and not adopted, are singleton births, and for whom all parental variables (including both parents' education) are observed.

identification.source_of_variation: The randomness of child gender: male-female differences in outcomes are compared across levels of mother's education, father's education and parental marital status at birth, which the paper describes as a difference-in-difference strategy (Eq. (1)).

key_assumptions.assumption: Child gender is independent of family environment (the randomness of child gender), so the male-family environment interaction identifies the causal effect of family environment on gender differences in outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2, which regresses an indicator for being male on observed family characteristics; the coefficients on parental education and marital status at birth are not jointly significantly different from zero

key_assumptions.assumption: Parental resources do not affect the endowments of boys and girls at birth differently, so the interaction reflects post-natal family environment rather than differences in endowments at birth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A.3, which shows that prenatal inputs and birth outcomes of sisters and brothers are not differently affected by the family environment

key_assumptions.assumption: The gender gap varies linearly and additively in the indicators of family environment, with no interaction between mother's and father's education or between family environment and marital status.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A.6 adds mother's x father's education interactions and Appendix Table A.7 adds family environment x marital status interactions, with F-tests of whether the additional interactions are jointly zero

behavioral spillovers between siblings and non-representativeness of families with gender-discordant siblings
